# Fibromyalgia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Rheumatology and immunology > Myopathies and pain syndromes > Fibromyalgia*

[Original Article Link](/library/2T0TJ2)

---

## Summary

Fibromyalgia is a chronic functional neurosensory disorder. The pathophysiology is notable for pervasive symptoms despite the absence of identifiable inflammation or structural changes on <u>physical exam</u>, imaging, or <u>histology</u>. Cardinal symptoms include diffuse chronic musculoskeletal <u>pain</u>, fatigue, and unrefreshing <u>sleep</u>. Cognitive dysfunction (often called <u>fibro fog</u>), <u>headaches</u>, and morning stiffness are also commonly reported. Individuals with fibromyalgia often have comorbid conditions with overlapping clinical features (e.g., <u>depressive disorders</u>, <u>migraine</u>, <u>irritable bowel syndrome</u>). Since objective findings cannot be used to confirm or rule out fibromyalgia, the diagnosis relies on a thorough history of symptoms (i.e., character, duration, and severity). Although fibromyalgia is not a progressive illness, it can cause significant functional limitations and <u>distress</u>. Step-wise treatment begins with patient education, especially pertaining to exercise for which there is strong evidence to support a therapeutic effect. Additional treatments (e.g., <u>physiotherapy</u> and pharmacological therapy) and multidisciplinary <u>pain management</u> can be considered using <u>shared decision-making</u>.

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>: 2–3%  [[1]](/library/T7Y6Oq)

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> (2:1) [[2]](/library/M7YMmq)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: : 20–50 years (risk of occurrence increases with age)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The pathophysiology of fibromyalgia is not fully understood; its etiology is likely multifactorial. The interaction of the following factors may play a role: [[3]](/library/0nae7O)




* <u>Central sensitization</u> and altered <u>pain</u> processing

* Genetic predisposition

* Autoimmune[[4]](/library/QS1uzT0)

* Environmental triggers (e.g., physical or psychosocial <u>stress</u>)

* Dysregulation of the neuroendocrine and <u>autonomic nervous systems</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Fibromyalgia is a <u>nociplastic pain</u> disorder where <u>pain</u> arises from altered <u>nociception</u> despite no clear tissue damage. It is driven by <u>central sensitization</u>, a 'functional rewiring' of the <u>CNS</u> that creates a state of Triple A: Amplification of <u>pain</u>, Allodynia (<u>pain</u> from <u>light touch</u>), and Augmentation of non-<u>pain</u> symptoms like fatigue and "<u>fibro fog</u>."'

---

## Clinical features

Fibromyalgia manifests with chronic functional symptoms. Symptoms and severity vary between individuals, ranging from mild and intermittent to persistent and disabling.




### Cardinal symptoms of fibromyalgia [[5]](/library/bC1HqQ0)[[6]](/library/1C12IQ0)




* Diffuse chronic musculoskeletal <u>pain</u>

* Distribution: all or most regions of the body

* Character: variable, often neuropathic, without objective pathologic findings

* Fatigue

* Unrefreshing <u>sleep</u>





### Common additional symptoms [[5]](/library/bC1HqQ0)




* Fibro fog: a form of cognitive dysfunction that includes difficulty concentrating and lack of clarity of thought

* <u>Headaches</u> (e.g., <u>migraine</u>)

* Morning stiffness

* <u>Paresthesias</u>

* <u>Memory</u> deficits

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> or cramps

* Autonomic changes

* <u>Xerostomia</u>, <u>xerophthalmia</u>

* Blurry <u>vision</u>, <u>photophobia</u>

* <u>Raynaud phenomenon</u>

* <u>Restless leg syndrome</u>

* <u>Pain</u> at tender points;  (used historically): 18 sites on the body, primarily where muscles and <u>tendons</u> attach to bone

---

## Diagnosis

The diagnosis of fibromyalgia is based on symptoms alone. Imaging studies and biomarkers (e.g., <u>ESR</u>) are typically normal.




### Clinical evaluation [[5]](/library/bC1HqQ0)




* Consider the diagnosis in patients with <u>cardinal symptoms of fibromyalgia</u> (± <u>fibro fog</u>) for ≥ 3 months.

* Assess for:

* Baseline impact on quality of life and functional status

* Alleviating and aggravating factors (e.g., <u>sensitivity</u> to cold or noise)

* Order <u>CBC</u> and either <u>ESR</u> or <u>CRP</u> to identify a concomitant inflammatory condition. [[7]](/library/x0WERP0)

* Limit additional studies to specific conditions being considered, e.g: [[7]](/library/x0WERP0)

* <u>Rheumatoid factor</u>, <u>antinuclear antibodies</u>, <u>myositis-specific antibodies</u>

* <u>Thyroid-stimulating hormone</u>

* <u>Sleep studies</u>

* Evaluation tools may help standardize the assessment but are not required for diagnosis.





> [!TIP]
> Eliciting <u>pain</u> at ≥ 11 of 18 <u>tender points</u> is a nonspecific finding and is no longer recommended in the assessment of fibromyalgia. [[7]](/library/x0WERP0)




> [!WARNING]
> Do not test patients for specific alternative conditions (e.g., <u>Lyme disease</u>) unless they have characteristic clinical features and appropriate history. [[8]](/library/cC1aIQ0)




### Evaluation tools [[5]](/library/bC1HqQ0)




Numerous diagnostic criteria and validated tools for screening and assessment have been proposed but are not required for diagnosis.




* Examples

* 2016 <u>ACR</u> diagnostic criteria

* Simplified Fibromyalgia Screening Questionnaire

* Patient Health Questionnaire-15

* Advantage: standardized assessments

* Limitation: debated and uncertain clinical utility

## Differential diagnoses

### Comorbid conditions [[7]](/library/x0WERP0)




Several conditions share prominent clinical features with fibromyalgia and often occur simultaneously, e.g.:




* Functional syndromes

* <u>Chronic fatigue syndrome</u>

* <u>Irritable bowel syndrome</u>

* <u>Migraine</u> or <u>tension headaches</u>

* <u>Chronic pelvic pain syndrome</u>, <u>bladder</u> syndromes

* Psychiatric disorders

* <u>Depressive disorders</u>

* <u>Generalized anxiety disorder</u>

* Inflammatory conditions

* <u>Systemic lupus erythematosus</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Fibromyalgia and conditions with overlapping symptoms are not mutually exclusive and can occur simultaneously. [[9]](/library/g7YFOq)




### Other




* <u>Polymyalgia rheumatica</u>

* <u>Hypothyroid myopathy</u>

* <u>Complex regional pain syndrome</u>

* <u>Sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Lyme disease</u>

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* See also “<u>Differential diagnoses of myopathies</u>.”





#### Myofascial pain syndrome




* Definition: : a <u>chronic pain</u> syndrome caused by muscle tension, injury, or repetitive motion and characterized by the presence of trigger points in muscles and/or <u>fascia</u> (small tender knots) [[10]](/library/n7Y7mq)

* Clinical features

* <u>Pain</u> is mostly confined to one anatomical region: fewer <u>tender points</u> compared to fibromyalgia (≤ 11 of 18)

* Leads to <u>weakness</u> and limited <u>range of motion</u>

* Jump sign (myofascial pain syndrome): A <u>physical examination</u> finding characterized by an involuntary, sudden jerk or wince in response to stimulation of a tender area or trigger point (not seen in fibromyalgia).

* Fatigue, <u>headache</u>, and <u>sleep</u> disturbances are less frequent compared to fibromyalgia

* Treatment: <u>physical therapy</u>, massage, stretching, ice packs, <u>NSAIDs</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Approach




* Optimize patient education and supportive therapy for all patients.

* Consider adding pharmacotherapy for severe <u>pain</u> and/or <u>sleep</u> disturbance refractory to nonpharmacological measures.

* Engage a multidisciplinary team ; (e.g., rheumatology, <u>psychiatry</u>) for patients who do not achieve adequate relief.

* For patients with new, worsening, or changing <u>pain</u> seen in ambulatory and emergency settings:

* Follow the general approach to <u>acute-on-chronic pain management</u>.

* Avoid repeating extensive diagnostic testing that has already been done (especially involving radiation or invasive procedures).

* Consult the patient's regular provider(s) early and arrange follow-up.





### Patient education [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)




* Exercise: There is strong evidence to support the benefits of aerobic and strengthening exercises. [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)[[12]](/library/cA1aij0)

* Reassurance: Fibromyalgia is not a progressive illness and does not result from muscle or nerve damage.

* Validation: Symptoms can be overwhelming and disabling.

* <u>Coping strategies</u>, e.g., relaxation techniques

* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>

* See also “Patient encounters” in “<u>Managing chronic conditions</u>.”





### Supportive therapy [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)




* <u>Physiotherapy</u> (e.g., stretching, hydrotherapy, and <u>heat application</u>)

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* <u>Acupuncture</u>





### Pharmacological therapy [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)




* Severe <u>pain</u>: <u>pregabalin</u> DOSAGE and/or <u>duloxetine</u> DOSAGE and/or <u>tramadol</u> (<u>off-label</u>)  [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)

* <u>Sleep</u> disturbance: low dose <u>amitriptyline</u> and/or <u>cyclobenzaprine</u> and/or <u>pregabalin</u>  [[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>NSAIDs</u> and <u>opioids</u> (with the exception of <u>tramadol</u>) are generally ineffective and not recommended for the <u>treatment of fibromyalgia</u>. [[8]](/library/cC1aIQ0)[[11]](/library/6C1jGQ0)
